The Inaccessible Island Rail dwells in Atlantis, its two black feet planted upon the black plateau. It may be slight, it may be threadbare, yet it knows what it knows. Rain falls from the sky. In trying, the wind lends what aid it can. In time, the strangest things come to pass: a tunnel discovers itself within the grass, and eggs the color of milk, of lavender.

---

# The Rail of Inaccessible Island

On the black plateau of Atlantis, where the world seems to end at the edge of sheer cliffs, there lives a small and unassuming bird known as the Inaccessible Island Rail. It does not question its place in this remote world; it exists with a quiet, unshakable certainty, as though the harshness of its surroundings were simply the natural order of things—not a hardship to be endured, but the only reality it has ever known.

The environment here offers little comfort. Rain falls with regularity, and what sunshine does break through the heavy sky is fleeting and thin. Strong winds sweep constantly across the plateau, bending the grasses and testing the resilience of every living thing that dares to take root. And at the edges of this desolate stretch of land, the cliffs mark a boundary beyond which nothing seems to exist—a stark, final edge to the known world.

Amid this austere landscape grows the Island Cape Myrtle, a plant that carries within it a quiet tension between authenticity and imitation. It is, in essence, a false or lesser version of true myrtle—a stand-in, a shadow of something more genuine. The true Roman Myrtle, by contrast, exists only beyond the cliffs, in a place inaccessible to those confined to the plateau. This distinction between the real and the almost-real becomes a subtle undercurrent running through the island's story, a reminder that not everything which resembles the genuine article can claim to be it.

The Inaccessible Island Rails have adapted to this unforgiving terrain with quiet resourcefulness. They build their nests within boulders scarred by lightning, finding shelter in the very marks of nature's violence. Their diet consists of insects and plant material, whatever sustenance the sparse landscape can offer. And though they are not born knowing how to fly, they do not remain grounded forever—through persistent, patient effort, they gradually learn to lift themselves into the air, mastering a skill that does not come naturally but is earned through determination.

The landscape itself, dominated by grass and ferns, seems at first to promise little beyond survival. Yet even here, in this sparse and challenging terrain, delicate and unexpected phenomena find a way to emerge. Tunnels begin to form within the grass, hidden pathways carved out by persistent life. And the eggs the rails lay possess an unexpected beauty—colored in soft shades of milk and lavender, a quiet elegance that contrasts sharply with the starkness of the world around them.

In this way, the story of the Inaccessible Island Rail becomes more than a tale of survival. It is a testament to the quiet resilience of life, to the way beauty and progress can emerge even in the most isolated and difficult of places, and to the enduring tension between what is authentic and what merely imitates the real.

# The Rail of Inaccessible Island

Rain comes sideways here, driven by winds that have crossed a thousand miles of empty ocean with nothing to slow them until they meet these black volcanic cliffs. This is Atlantis—not the legend, but a peak thrust up from the South Atlantic, so remote that ships pass decades without sighting its shores. The island wears its isolation like armor, and few creatures have ever managed to breach it.

Yet here, in the tussock grass and stunted fern-bush, something small persists.

The Inaccessible Island Rail measures scarcely more than a clenched fist, dark feathers the color of wet stone, wings so reduced by generations of flightlessness that they serve no purpose but memory. It cannot soar above the cliffs or ride the wind to easier ground. It can only walk, low and quick, through the tangled heath where the Island Cape Myrtle grows—a shrub that borrows its name from distant continents but belongs entirely to this place, twisted by salt wind into shapes that mock its elegant name.

The bird forages where lesser creatures would starve: overturning stones for beetles, picking at the sparse insects that cling to leeward leaves, working through vegetation stunted by wind and poverty of soil. Every meal is small. Every day demands the same patient searching, the same narrow survival wrung from an unforgiving terrain.

And yet, from this relentless smallness comes something unexpected.

Watch how the rail moves—not flying, but flowing, low to the ground with a swiftness that mimics flight, wings half-spread for balance, feet barely touching earth. In this urgent scuttle across the wind-scoured heath there is a kind of grace, a transmutation of struggle into rhythm, of hardship into a strange and specific beauty.

Deeper in the grass, hidden from wind and eye alike, the rail builds its nest: a woven tunnel of dried stalks, domed and secret, opening only to a narrow entrance no predator could easily find. Inside wait eggs—pale, delicate, impossibly soft against the harsh volcanic backdrop that birthed them. They seem to belong to some gentler world, though they exist only because of this hard one.

This is the quiet miracle of Inaccessible Island: that in a place named for its very unreachability, in soil scarred by fire and scoured by ceaseless rain, something so fragile continues to hatch, to walk, to endure. The rail asks nothing of the world beyond what the island offers—insects, grass, shelter from wind—and in return, it offers proof that even in the most forgotten corners of the earth, life finds its narrow way through, hidden and persistent and quietly wondrous.

# The Inaccessible Island

Far beyond the reach of common shipping lanes, where the ocean stretches in every direction without interruption, there exists a small volcanic outcropping that has earned its name through simple, unforgiving geography. The Inaccessible Island rises sharply from the sea, its cliffs plunging directly into churning waters with almost no natural harbor to welcome visitors. There are no beaches to speak of, no gentle slopes where boats might safely land. Instead, the island presents a fortress-like face to anyone who dares approach.

This isolation has made the island a subject of fascination for naturalists and adventurers alike. Because human visitors have been so rare throughout history, the ecosystem here evolved largely undisturbed. Endemic species—found nowhere else on Earth—have flourished in this natural laboratory of evolution. Flightless birds wander through tussock grass unafraid of predators they've never known. Unique insects and plant life cling to volcanic soil, having adapted to conditions found only on this remote speck of land.

The few expeditions that have successfully landed required careful planning, favorable weather, and no small amount of luck. Even then, researchers often found themselves stranded for longer than intended, waiting for the seas to calm enough to permit departure. The island's inaccessibility, while a challenge for science, has proven to be its greatest protector—shielding it from the introduction of invasive species, from exploitation, and from the changes that human presence inevitably brings.

In an age where satellite imagery has mapped nearly every corner of our planet, places like this remain strangely mysterious. We can see the island from above, chart its coastline with precision, and study its vegetation through remote sensing, yet the experience of standing upon its volcanic rock remains reserved for the very few willing to brave its unwelcoming shores. Perhaps this is fitting—some places, it seems, are meant to remain just beyond our grasp, preserving both their ecology and their mystery in equal measure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about the Inaccessible Island Rail and its remote habitat on Inaccessible Island.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rail's Inheritance

On an island named for its own refusal, the smallest flightless bird in the world practices the art of staying. It has forgotten the sky the way we forget the taste of milk—completely, gratefully, as evolution's mercy. Wings became suggestions, then vestiges, then a kind of punctuation the body makes when it has nowhere left to fly to.

The island rises from the South Atlantic like a held breath, all cliffs and tussock grass and the particular loneliness of latitude 37°17′S, where no ships stop and no calendars matter. Here the fog performs its slow choreography, wrapping around volcanic rock that remembers fire the way old men remember wars—reluctantly, and only when the weather turns.

The rail moves through this world in fits and starts, a small brown comma punctuating sentences the ferns write in wind. It has three cousins on the mainland, extinct now, ghosts folded into museum drawers, their taxidermy eyes still startled by cameras that stopped flashing decades ago. But this one remains, this last uncle of a vanished family, scratching through leaf litter for insects that don't know they're being hunted by something that time forgot to finish erasing.

Consider the improbability: a bird that cannot fly, alone on rock that cannot be reached, thriving precisely because the world could not be bothered to find it. Inaccessibility as sanctuary. Isolation as inheritance. The island's cruelty—its cliffs, its indifference, its refusal of harbors—becomes the very fence that keeps extinction at bay.

At dusk, when the light goes the color of old rust, the rail calls out—not a song exactly, more a small assertion against the enormous quiet. *I am here*, it seems to say, to no one, to the fog, to the ghosts of its mainland cousins, to the sea that guards this place like a mother who has already lost too many children.

The grass bends. The bird does not fly. The island keeps its secret the way all sacred things do: by being nearly impossible to find, and once found, impossible to forget.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, fragmented piece of writing that blends natural history facts about a rare flightless bird with dreamlike, mythic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**GHOST OF THE RIMU: A KĀKĀPŌ ABECEDARY**

*i.*

They say it forgot how to fly the way a man forgets his mother tongue—
slowly, then all at once, then only in dreams.

Moss-feathered. Owl-faced. A parrot wearing the shape of night.
*Strigops habroptilus*: the soft-feathered one, the one who does not sing so much as *drum the world awake.*

*ii.*

Fact: the kākāpō is the heaviest parrot alive, and the only one who cannot lift itself into the sky.
Fact: it smells of honey and old wood, a scent trackers call *sweet, musty, floral*—as if it were rotting into blossom.
Fact: there are fewer than two hundred left, and each one has a name, a number, a tiny radio heart stitched beneath its skin.

*iii.*

In the old telling, the bird was punished for standing still while the others learned the sky.
The gods said: *you loved the ground too much,* and took the wind from under it.
Now it walks the forest like a green ghost, freezing when frightened, mistaking stillness for invisibility—
believing, still, that if it does not move, the hawk above cannot see it.

*iv.*

Only the rimu tree decides when love may happen.
Once every two, three, four years, the fruit falls heavy and sweet, and the males dig bowls into the earth—
*track and bowl systems*, the scientists call them, as if it were architecture and not longing.

They sit in their carved hollows and boom.
A low sound, a heartbeat sound, thrown for kilometers through the dark,
a subsonic hymn that says *come find me* though he cannot say where *here* is,
though the females wander the black hills listening for a sound that seems to come from everywhere and nowhere,
the way a name called in a dream comes from inside your own chest.

*v.*

Myth: the moon fell in love with a flightless bird and taught it to boom instead of fly,
so its longing would still reach the sky, if nothing else could.

Fact: he may boom for a hundred nights and mate with none.
Fact: this is not tragedy. This is simply how the rimu, the moon, and the waiting have always worked.

*vi.*

Before the ships came, before the claws and teeth of animals it had never dreamed of,
the kākāpō walked an island with no reason to be afraid.
It unlearned fear the way it unlearned flight—
a slow surrender to a gentler world that could not last.

*vii.*

Now the survivors live on islands without predators, tracked, weighed, fed by hand,
each one a small mossy god kept alive by clipboards and prayer.

They call this *conservation.*
The old stories would call it something else—
a tribe of green ghosts, kept just this side of myth,
waiting for the rimu to fruit again,
waiting to boom the moon down from the sky,
waiting, in their strange patient stillness,
to be forgiven for staying too long in love with the ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic description of an isolated island ecosystem, weaving in details about endemic plants like Island Cape Myrtle and the birds that live among them.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Isolate

Where salt-wind carves the cliffs to bone
and no bridge remembers the mainland's name,
the island keeps its own quiet parliament—
a green republic, self-declared, self-sustained.

Here, the Island Cape Myrtle roots
in soil no other hand has sown,
its leathery leaves like small green shields
against the Atlantic's endless throne.
White blossoms open only to this light,
this particular slant of morning sun—
found nowhere else beneath the sky,
a fingerprint pressed on stone.

The birds arrived by accident or will,
storm-blown or star-guided, who can say—
and stayed until their wings forgot
the long roads back, the mainland way.
Now they nest in myrtle's tangled arms,
their calls evolved to fit this narrow world:
a song shaped by isolation's hand,
notes no distant forest ever heard.

Watch how the flightless rail still runs
through shadows the ancestors once flew—
how caution loosened into trust
when nothing came to hunt or chase or pursue.
Watch the finch whose beak has changed
to fit the seedpod of the myrtle tree,
a slow negotiation with the land,
a marriage of necessity.

This is what isolation makes:
not poverty, but strange, precise abundance—
a thousand tiny fits and starts
toward some unrepeatable accordance.
Lose this rock, and lose forever
the particular grammar of this life,
the singular answer this island gives
to the old, old question: *how to survive*.

So let the ferry come but rarely.
Let the isolation hold.
Some things exist by staying separate—
some fires burn because they're small, not bold.
Here, myrtle and bird and stone conspire
in a language only this place speaks—
a fragile, radiant translation
of what the whole earth, once, might have seen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental, imagistic poem in short declarative sentences about a small flightless bird surviving on a windswept island plateau.
counterfactuals.output:
**Plateau Bird**

The wind arrives first. It always arrives first.

The bird has no memory of sky.
Its wings are stubs. Its wings are almost nothing.

Grass leans one direction only.
The bird leans with it.

*

Morning is gray felt pulled over stone.
The bird walks through tussock, head low.

Its feet are orange. Its feet are the only orange thing here.

A beetle. The bird eats the beetle.
The wind eats the sound of eating.

*

Fog comes up from the cliffs like breath from a mouth.
The bird does not flinch. The bird has never flinched.

Its eye is black. Its eye holds the whole plateau
and gives nothing back.

*

Night drops without a sunset.
There is no sunset here, only less light.

The bird presses into a crevice.
Stone remembers the day's small warmth. Barely.

Its heartbeat is fast. Its heartbeat is the fastest thing
for a hundred miles.

*

Storms come sideways.
The bird becomes a stone among stones.

Feathers salt-stiff. Feathers holding.
The world tries to erase it. The world fails.

*

Spring, if it comes, comes gray-green.
The bird finds an egg-shaped silence in itself
and sits on it.

*

Years pass like weather passes.
The bird does not count them.

It has only this: rock, wind, orange feet,
the black unblinking eye,
the body that stays low
and does not fly
and does not die.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of nature writing with a stream-of-consciousness, almost mythological tone about a rare bird species, its diet, environment, and the strange beauty of its isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Night Parrot, Who Is Barely a Rumor**

Before there was a name for it there was only the sound—not a call so much as a small held breath escaping the spinifex, a psst-psst-ooing that traveled through red dust like a secret passed hand to hand and then denied by everyone who touched it. They say the bird is green and yellow and black, mottled like the underside of a leaf that has learned to be stone, and they say this because someone, once, in 1912 or 1979 or some other century that has already forgotten itself, held a dead one in their palms and wrote it down before the desert took the knowledge back.

It lives—if *lives* is even the verb, if presence counts as living when it is ninety-nine parts absence—in the spinifex hummocks of the interior, that country which does not perform itself for anyone, which offers no vista, no postcard, only heat shimmering off itself in circles like a held note. The spinifex grows in wheels, in green-gold fists clenched around a center, and inside those fists, in tunnels no wider than thought, the night parrot makes its cathedral. It does not fly so much as it disappears—rising just enough to clear the spikes, dropping again before the sky can properly notice it, before the wedge-tailed shadow above can translate absence into meal.

By day it is a held breath. By night it becomes an appetite.

It eats the seeds of the samphire, the succulent chenopod, the spinifex's own hard grain—small closed fists of nutrition that it must crack and know in darkness, moving by memory and smell and some older sense we have no word for because we have not needed it, having given up the dark long ago for our fires and our screens. It walks more than it flies. It runs low through the understory like something that remembers being reptile, something that has not fully agreed to the sky's terms.

Water it takes from claypans that exist for three days a year, then vanish, becoming just another name for absence—*ephemeral*, the hydrologists call it, a word that could describe the bird itself, the species, the whole fragile hypothesis of its continuing to exist.

For a hundred years there was only the museum skin, the "possibly extinct," the mounted specter in glass that ornithologists visited like pilgrims visiting a saint's finger-bone—reverent, doubtful, aching for a resurrection they didn't believe would come. And then: 2013. A camera trap. A green blur in infrared, caught mid-stride, entering the spinifex like a soul entering the mouth of the world. Grown men wept, they say. Grown men who had spent careers doubting suddenly had to believe in something, and belief, after such a drought, tastes like the first rain on a claypan—shocking, holy, brief.

This is the strange beauty of it: that isolation is not the opposite of miracle but its precondition. The bird is rare *because* the country is merciless, and the country's mercilessness is the only reason the bird survived at all—ferals and foxes and cats slowed by heat, by distance, by the same red immensity that starves the bird of easy food. Its secrecy is not a failure to be found. It is a strategy perfected over ten thousand years of learning that visibility is death, that the wide sky belongs to raptors, and the only safety is to become a rumor with feathers, a green psalm sung once at dusk and then swallowed whole by grass.

We will likely never see it. This is, perhaps, correct. Some things are not meant for our witnessing but only for our knowing-of, the way we know of gods we've never met, ancestors we never touched, the pulse of something vast and old moving just beyond the campfire's light. The night parrot asks only this: that the spinifex keep its wheel-shape, that the claypans keep their brief holy water, that the dark stay dark enough for a small green weight to move through it, cracking seeds in its beak like a monk telling beads, keeping some old testament alive in a language none of us were ever meant to speak.
